q: Machine P has a present value of total costs of Rs 7,20,000 with an annuity factor of 3.600 for its life, and Machine Q a present value of total costs of Rs 8,25,000 with an annuity factor of 3.000 for its life. Both render the same service. On the equivalent annual cost basis, the correct choice and figures are:

options.A: P, whose equivalent annual cost of Rs 2,00,000 is below Q's Rs 2,75,000
options.B: Q, whose equivalent annual cost of Rs 2,75,000 is below P's Rs 2,00,000
options.C: P, because its present value of total costs is the lower of the two
options.D: Q, because its life, as shown by the smaller annuity factor, is the shorter

q: The equivalent annual cost of an asset, computed for each possible length of life, is: 1 year — Rs 2,10,000; 2 years — Rs 1,95,000; 3 years — Rs 1,88,000; 4 years — Rs 1,92,000; 5 years — Rs 1,99,000. The economic life of the asset is:

options.A: 1 year
options.B: 3 years
options.C: 4 years
options.D: 5 years

q: A defender can be sold now for Rs 80,000 or, after one more year of service, for Rs 60,000. Running it for that further year will cost Rs 95,000 in cash operating costs. The equivalent annual cost of the best challenger is Rs 1,10,000. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Keep the defender, because its cash operating cost of Rs 95,000 is below Rs 1,10,000
options.B: Keep the defender, because the fall in its salvage value is only Rs 20,000
options.C: Remain indifferent, the two courses being equal in cost
options.D: Replace now, because the cost of keeping the defender for one more year, Rs 1,15,000, exceeds the challenger's equivalent annual cost

q: The optimum replacement cycle of an asset is reached at the life at which:

options.A: The total undiscounted cost of owning the asset is the lowest
options.B: The salvage value of the asset falls to zero
options.C: The equivalent annual cost of the asset is at its minimum
options.D: The annual operating cost first begins to rise

q: In judging whether the defender should be retained, its current realisable (salvage) value enters the analysis as:

options.A: A sunk amount to be ignored altogether
options.B: An opportunity cost of retention, being the cash forgone by not selling it now
options.C: A cash inflow of the retention alternative in the final year only
options.D: A deduction from the original cost of the defender

q: A replacement decision is properly made by comparing:

options.A: The incremental cash flows of replacing now with those of retaining the defender
options.B: The accounting profits reported under the two alternatives
options.C: The book values of the defender and the challenger
options.D: The total costs of the challenger with the original cost of the defender

q: The defender-versus-challenger comparison has to be repeated afresh at each successive replacement point chiefly because:

options.A: The cost of capital changes every year by rule
options.B: Depreciation methods are revised annually
options.C: Tax rates are re-enacted every year
options.D: The challenger available later may be a better asset, and the defender's salvage value and running costs change with age

q: Project P requires Rs 4,00,000 with a present value of inflows of Rs 5,00,000; Project Q requires Rs 6,00,000 with a present value of inflows of Rs 7,20,000; Project R requires Rs 5,00,000 with a present value of inflows of Rs 6,50,000. Ranked by Profitability Index, the order of preference is:

options.A: P, Q, R
options.B: Q, P, R
options.C: R, P, Q
options.D: R, Q, P

q: Funds of Rs 14,00,000 are available and the competing projects are divisible. Project C requires Rs 6,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 2,10,000, Project A requires Rs 9,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 2,70,000 and Project B requires Rs 8,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 2,00,000. Ranked by Net Present Value per rupee invested, C and A are taken first, A being taken in part to use up the funds. The total Net Present Value of the combination so selected is:

Funds available are Rs 18,00,000 and the projects are indivisible. Project A requires Rs 10,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 3,00,000, Project B requires Rs 8,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 2,80,000, Project C requires Rs 9,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 2,70,000 and Project D requires Rs 7,00,000 with a Net Present Value of Rs 1,90,000. The combination that maximises the total Net Present Value within the funds available is:

options.A: A and B, with a total Net Present Value of Rs 5,80,000
options.B: B and C, with a total Net Present Value of Rs 5,50,000
options.C: A and D, with a total Net Present Value of Rs 4,90,000
options.D: C and D, with a total Net Present Value of Rs 4,60,000

q: Multi-period capital rationing differs from single-period capital rationing in that, in the multi-period case:

options.A: The Profitability Index alone gives the complete solution
options.B: Funds are constrained in two or more successive periods, so a project acceptable in the first period may be blocked by the shortage of a later period
options.C: Projects are assumed to be divisible in all cases
options.D: No discounting of cash flows is required

q: At the concept level, the linear programming approach to capital rationing is used in order to:

options.A: Compute the internal rate of return of a combined programme
options.B: Rank projects by payback period under a single constraint
options.C: Select the combination of projects that maximises the total Net Present Value subject to the funds constraints of each period
options.D: Replace the Net Present Value rule for individual projects

q: Ranking by Profitability Index can fail to give the best selection of projects when:

options.A: The projects are indivisible, so that the highest-ranked combination may leave funds unused which a lower-ranked combination could employ profitably
options.B: The projects are divisible and can be taken up in fractions
options.C: All the projects require the same initial outlay
options.D: The discount rate used is the cost of capital

q: Capital rationing imposed by factors outside the enterprise, such as an inability to raise funds in the capital market on acceptable terms, is described as:

options.A: Soft rationing
options.B: Internal rationing
options.C: Self-imposed rationing
options.D: Hard rationing

q: Where projects are indivisible and no combination exactly exhausts the funds available, the unspent balance under the best combination should be:

options.A: Forced into the next project on the ranking list regardless of its return
options.B: Judged by what it can earn elsewhere, the best feasible combination being the one with the highest total Net Present Value
options.C: Treated as a loss equal to its full amount
options.D: Added to the Net Present Value of the selected projects

q: An asset costing Rs 10,00,000 can instead be leased for 5 years at an annual rental of Rs 2,60,000 payable at each year-end. The tax rate is 30 per cent, rentals are tax-deductible, straight-line depreciation of Rs 2,00,000 a year would be forgone on leasing, and the annuity factor for 5 years at the after-tax cost of debt is 4.100. The Net Advantage of Leasing is:

options.A: (-) Rs 7,800, so buying is preferable
options.B: (+) Rs 2,53,800, rentals alone being compared with the cost
options.C: (+) Rs 7,800, so leasing is marginally preferable
options.D: Nil, the two courses being exactly equal

q: An asset is leased at an annual rental of Rs 1,50,000 for 5 years, the rental being fully tax-deductible and the tax rate 30 per cent. The annuity factor for 5 years at the appropriate discount rate is 3.605. The present value of the after-tax lease rentals is:
In a lease-versus-buy appraisal, the after-tax lease rentals and the forgone depreciation tax shield are ordinarily discounted at:

options.A: The cost of equity of the lessee
options.B: The internal rate of return of the asset
options.C: The risk-free rate in all circumstances
options.D: The after-tax cost of debt, leasing being essentially a financing alternative comparable to borrowing

q: A positive Net Advantage of Leasing arises in practice mainly because:

options.A: Lease rentals are never subject to tax in the lessee's hands
options.B: Of tax and financing asymmetries between lessor and lessee, so that the lessor can pass on part of the benefit of the depreciation and interest tax shields in lower rentals
options.C: The lessee avoids all operating risk of the asset under every lease
options.D: The purchase price of the asset is ignored in the comparison

q: Under a sale-and-leaseback arrangement, an enterprise:

options.A: Sells an asset it owns to a lessor and takes the same asset back on lease, releasing the capital locked up in it while retaining its use
options.B: Sells an asset outright and purchases a different asset on lease
options.C: Leases an asset to another enterprise and buys it back at the end
options.D: Buys an asset with borrowed funds and sells it to the lender

q: The sound sequence for a lease-versus-buy decision is to:

options.A: Decide the financing first and appraise the investment afterwards
options.B: Treat the rental as an operating cost and ignore the purchase price
options.C: First judge the asset as an investment on its own merits, and only then compare leasing with borrowing-and-buying as rival ways of financing it
options.D: Compare the total undiscounted rentals with the purchase price

q: An asset is leased at an annual rental of Rs 1,00,000, fully tax-deductible, the tax rate being 35 per cent. The annuity factor for the lease term at the appropriate discount rate is 3.605. The present value of the after-tax lease rentals is:
A lease under which the lessor bears the maintenance and insurance of the asset, the term is short in relation to the asset's life and the lease can ordinarily be cancelled, is in substance:

options.A: A finance lease
options.B: An operating lease
options.C: A leveraged lease
options.D: A sale-and-leaseback

q: The Net Advantage of Leasing is computed as:

options.A: The cost of the asset avoided on leasing, minus the present value of the after-tax lease rentals and the present value of the depreciation tax shield forgone
options.B: The total lease rentals minus the purchase price of the asset
options.C: The present value of the lease rentals minus the depreciation of the asset
options.D: The purchase price minus the undiscounted total of the rentals

q: When an asset is leased instead of bought, the depreciation tax shield is forgone by the lessee because:

options.A: Depreciation is disallowed on all leased assets by the tax law in every case
options.B: The lessee claims the rentals twice over
options.C: Ownership, and with it the depreciation allowance, rests with the lessor, who claims the shield instead
options.D: A leased asset has no depreciable value at all

q: A post-audit (post-completion audit) of a capital project is carried out in order to:

options.A: Recover the amount overspent on the project from the sponsoring department
options.B: Re-open the original sanction of the project
options.C: Cancel projects whose actual returns fall below the estimates
options.D: Compare the actual costs, benefits and completion time with the estimates on which the project was sanctioned, and feed the lessons back into future appraisals

q: A post-audit loses most of its usefulness if it is conducted as:

options.A: A review by officers not associated with the original appraisal
options.B: A fault-finding and punitive exercise, which tempts sponsoring managers to pad future estimates defensively
options.C: A comparison of actual results with the sanctioned estimates
options.D: A source of feedback for improving estimating techniques

q: For the post-audit comparison to be meaningful, the actual results of a project should be compared with:

options.A: The results of an unrelated project of similar size
options.B: The revised estimates prepared after the project was completed
options.C: The original estimates and assumptions recorded at the time of sanction, adjusted only for clearly identified changes outside the project's control
options.D: The budget provision made for the project in its final year

q: A systematic benefit which post-auditing is expected to confer on the appraisal process itself is that:

options.A: Knowing that out-turn will be checked against their estimates, project sponsors are induced to submit more realistic estimates in the first place
options.B: The cost of capital of the enterprise falls automatically
options.C: Every project appraised thereafter shows a positive Net Present Value
options.D: The need for discounting future cash flows is removed

q: An abandonment decision — closing down or selling off a project before the end of its planned life — should be taken when:

options.A: The project's book value has fallen below its original cost
options.B: The project has reported an accounting loss in any one year
options.C: The abandonment has been provided for in the original estimates
options.D: The amount realisable on abandonment exceeds the present value of the cash flows from continuing the project

q: A project has a book value of Rs 4,00,000 and can be sold at once for Rs 3,40,000, the loss on sale being allowed for tax at 30 per cent. The present value of the cash flows from continuing it is Rs 3,30,000. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Continue, because the sale price is below the book value
options.B: Abandon, because the after-tax abandonment proceeds of Rs 3,58,000 exceed the present value of continuing
options.C: Continue, because the present value of continuing exceeds the sale price net of book value
options.D: Remain indifferent, the two values being equal

q: The abandonment value of a project is relevant at every stage of its life because it represents:

options.A: The original cost of the project written down by depreciation
options.B: The amount that must be recovered before any profit is earned
options.C: An opportunity value — the cash given up by continuing the project instead of realising that value now
options.D: A reserve to be created out of the project's profits

q: A project can be sold at once for Rs 3,00,000 free of tax complications. If continued, it will yield a cash inflow after tax of Rs 1,20,000 at the end of each of the next 3 years, the annuity factor for 3 years at the cost of capital being 2.402. The correct decision is to:

options.A: Abandon, because the sale proceeds of Rs 3,00,000 exceed the present value of continuing, Rs 2,88,240
options.B: Continue, because the total undiscounted inflows of Rs 3,60,000 exceed the sale proceeds
options.C: Continue, because a project once sanctioned must run its full life
options.D: Abandon, because the annual inflow is less than half the sale proceeds

q: In an abandonment appraisal, the unrecovered book value of the project's assets, to the extent it cannot be realised or set off for tax, is:

options.A: A cash outflow of the continuation alternative
options.B: To be added to the abandonment proceeds
options.C: Recovered through the depreciation charge of the final year
options.D: A sunk amount, relevant only through any tax relief the loss on abandonment carries

q: A project has a Net Present Value of Rs 3,42,000 and the cumulative present value (annuity) factor for its life at the cost of capital is 3.800. Its equivalent annual annuity is:

A replacement requires additional working capital of Rs 75,000 at the start, recoverable in full at the end of Year 5, the present value factor for Year 5 at the cost of capital being 0.621. In the Net Present Value computation, this working capital affects the appraisal by:

options.A: An outflow of Rs 75,000 with no corresponding inflow at any stage
options.B: A net present cost of Rs 28,425, being the outflow of Rs 75,000 less the present value, Rs 46,575, of its recovery
options.C: A net present benefit of Rs 46,575, the initial outflow being a book entry
options.D: Nothing at all, working capital being excluded from replacement appraisals

q: Keeping a defender for one more year will require an overhaul costing Rs 40,000 at the start of the year, cash operating costs of Rs 60,000 during the year, and its salvage value will fall from Rs 90,000 to Rs 70,000 over the year. The equivalent annual cost of the best challenger is Rs 1,05,000. Ignoring discounting within the single year, the correct decision is to:

options.A: Keep the defender, its total cost of Rs 1,00,000 excluding the salvage fall being the lower figure
options.B: Keep the defender, because the overhaul will extend its life indefinitely
options.C: Remain indifferent, the two courses costing the same
options.D: Replace now, because the full cost of one more year of the defender, Rs 1,20,000, exceeds the challenger's equivalent annual cost of Rs 1,05,000

q: A challenger will save labour cost of Rs 1,80,000 a year but will cost Rs 30,000 a year more in maintenance. Depreciation will rise by Rs 50,000 a year and the tax rate is 25 per cent. The incremental annual cash inflow after tax of the replacement is:
A project was sanctioned at an estimated cost of Rs 50,00,000 and was completed at an actual cost of Rs 58,00,000. The percentage overrun on cost revealed by the post-audit is:

options.A: 13.8 per cent
options.B: 8.0 per cent
options.C: 16.0 per cent
options.D: 58.0 per cent

q: To preserve the credibility of a post-audit, it should ordinarily be carried out by:

options.A: The same officers who prepared the original estimates, acting alone
options.B: The contractor who executed the project
options.C: The sponsoring department without any accounts participation
options.D: Officers independent of the original appraisal and execution, so that the comparison of out-turn with estimates is objective

q: A multi-column flexible budget prepared for a production department is most useful to management because it:

options.A: Freezes the cost allowance at the single output level originally planned, whatever output is later achieved
options.B: Shows side by side the budgeted cost at several volumes of output, so the allowance matching the volume actually achieved can be read off directly
options.C: Records only the fixed costs of the department, variable costs being excluded from budgeting altogether
options.D: Replaces the need for any comparison of actual cost with budgeted cost at the end of the period

q: Maintenance cost was Rs 96,000 at an output of 8,000 units and Rs 1,28,000 at an output of 12,000 units. Applying the high-low method, the budgeted maintenance cost at an output of 10,000 units is:
Power and repair cost at 6,000 machine hours was Rs 54,000 and at 10,000 machine hours was Rs 74,000. Segregating the cost by the high-low method, the fixed element contained in it is:
Where past cost records at many different volumes are available, the method of segregating a semi-variable cost that uses all the observations, and not merely the highest and lowest, is:

options.A: The high-low method applied to two selected periods only
options.B: Apportionment of the total cost in the ratio of direct wages
options.C: Treating the whole semi-variable cost as fixed in every budget
options.D: The method of least squares, fitting a cost line through all the recorded observations

q: Fixed overhead is Rs 60,000, variable cost is Rs 12 per unit, and a semi-variable cost contains a fixed element of Rs 10,000 plus Rs 3 per unit. In a flexible budget, the total cost at 5,000 units is:
Variable overhead is budgeted at Rs 6 per hour and fixed overhead at Rs 48,000 for the period. The flexed overhead allowance for a month in which 9,000 hours are worked is:

A department works at 60 per cent of capacity against a fixed budget prepared at 90 per cent, and its total cost is well below the fixed budget figure. Judging its performance from that comparison alone would be misleading because:

options.A: Much of the apparent saving is simply the variable cost of the output that was never produced, and not efficiency in producing what was made
options.B: Fixed costs always fall in exact proportion to output
options.C: A fixed budget automatically restates itself for the output achieved
options.D: Variable costs do not change with the level of activity

q: A step cost, such as the salary of an additional supervisor needed for every extra shift, is best handled in a flexible budget by:

options.A: Treating it as varying uniformly with every single unit of output
options.B: Ignoring it, since it is neither wholly fixed nor wholly variable
options.C: Spreading it evenly over all levels of activity in the budget
options.D: Showing it as unchanged within each stated activity band and jumping to the higher amount when output crosses into the next band

q: The scattergraph method of segregating semi-variable costs proceeds by:

options.A: Solving simultaneous equations from the costs of two periods only
options.B: Plotting past costs against past volumes, drawing the line of best fit by inspection, and reading the fixed cost where the line meets the cost axis
options.C: Averaging the fixed costs reported by all departments of the factory
options.D: Deducting the standard cost of output from the actual cost incurred

q: For proper control, the actual cost of a department for a period should be compared with:

options.A: The original fixed budget, even where actual output differs widely from the budgeted output
options.B: The actual cost of the corresponding period of the previous year only
options.C: The flexed budget allowance for the level of activity actually attained during the period
options.D: The lowest cost recorded by any comparable department in any earlier year

q: Control ratios are computed in budgetary control primarily in order to:

options.A: Express performance in hours and working days as percentages, so that departures from the budgeted level of activity and efficiency can be seen at a glance
options.B: Convert all budgeted costs directly into selling prices
options.C: Replace the profit and loss account of the enterprise
options.D: Fix the standard time allowed for each operation on the shop floor

q: The activity ratio is correctly defined as:

options.A: Actual hours worked divided by budgeted hours, expressed as a percentage
options.B: Actual working days divided by budgeted working days, expressed as a percentage
options.C: Standard hours for actual output divided by actual hours worked, expressed as a percentage
options.D: Standard hours for actual output divided by budgeted hours, expressed as a percentage

q: Budgeted hours for a period are 10,000 and the standard hours for the output actually produced are 9,200. The activity ratio is:

options.A: 108.7 per cent
options.B: 92 per cent
options.C: 100 per cent
options.D: 84 per cent

q: Budgeted hours are 11,000 and the hours actually worked are 8,800. The capacity ratio is:

options.A: 125 per cent
options.B: 75 per cent
options.C: 80 per cent
options.D: 88 per cent

q: The standard hours for the output achieved are 8,550 and the hours actually taken are 9,000. The efficiency ratio is:

options.A: 95 per cent
options.B: 105.3 per cent
options.C: 90 per cent
options.D: 100 per cent

q: A factory was budgeted to work 25 days in a month but actually worked 24 days. Its calendar ratio for the month is:

options.A: 104.2 per cent
options.B: 100 per cent
options.C: 92 per cent
options.D: 96 per cent

q: Budgeted hours are 10,000, hours actually worked are 8,000, and the standard hours for the output produced are 10,000. The activity ratio is:

options.A: 80 per cent
options.B: 100 per cent
options.C: 125 per cent
options.D: 64 per cent

q: An efficiency ratio above 100 per cent in a period indicates that:

options.A: More hours were worked than were budgeted for the period
options.B: More working days were available than the budget had assumed
options.C: The output was produced in fewer actual hours than the standard hours allowed for it
options.D: Output in the period was higher than the budgeted output

q: Fixed cost is Rs 90,000 and variable cost is Rs 20 per unit. Normal capacity is 10,000 units. In the flexible budget, the total cost at 80 per cent of capacity is:
Total cost was Rs 54,000 at 3,000 units and Rs 74,000 at 5,000 units, cost behaviour remaining unchanged. The flexible budget allowance at 4,500 units is:
In a well-organised budgetary control system, the budget committee is expected to:

options.A: Prepare personally the detailed estimates of every department without consulting the managers concerned
options.B: Receive and examine the functional budget estimates, resolve conflicts between them, and recommend the co-ordinated budget for approval
options.C: Audit the budget variances after the close of the financial year
options.D: Fix the wages payable to workers in each department

q: A conflict arises between the sales budget and the production budget over the volume that can be sold and made. Within the budgetary control organisation, this conflict is ordinarily settled by:

options.A: The internal auditor, in the course of the annual audit
options.B: Leaving each department to follow its own unrevised estimate
options.C: The budget committee, after hearing both functions, subject to the limits set by the principal budget factor
options.D: The stores department, by adjusting the level of stocks held

q: Besides the timetable and the responsibilities of budget centres, a complete budget manual should also set out:

options.A: The procedure for revising budgets, the forms and reports to be used, and the manner in which variances are to be reported and followed up
options.B: The names of the customers to whom goods may be sold on credit
options.C: The detailed engineering drawings of every product made by the enterprise
options.D: The leave rules applicable to the clerical staff of the accounts office

q: A long-term budget covering, say, five to ten years is of limited precision mainly because:

options.A: No manager is responsible for any period beyond one year
options.B: Budgets can never be expressed for a period longer than twelve months
options.C: Capital budgets cannot be prepared for more than one year at a time
options.D: Conditions, prices and demand so far ahead can only be forecast broadly, so such budgets state plans in outline and are detailed only for the nearer years

q: In a season when the supply of a key raw material is severely restricted, the principal budget factor for the enterprise becomes:

options.A: The selling capacity of the sales force
options.B: The capacity of the plant installed in the factory
options.C: The quantity of that raw material obtainable, to which the production and sales budgets must both be keyed
options.D: The amount of cash standing in the bank account

q: Where anticipated demand for the product is the principal budget factor, the preparation of the functional budgets properly begins with:

options.A: The production budget, demand being fitted to factory capacity afterwards
options.B: The sales budget, the other functional budgets being built upon the sales forecast
options.C: The cash budget, since cash governs every other estimate
options.D: The capital expenditure budget for new plant

q: Half-way through the budget period the factor that had limited the budget ceases to operate and a different factor becomes limiting. The correct budgetary response is to:

options.A: Recast the affected functional budgets around the new limiting factor and obtain approval for the revised co-ordinated budget
options.B: Continue with the original budgets unchanged, since a budget once approved can never be altered
options.C: Abandon budgetary control for the remainder of the period
options.D: Report the change only in the annual accounts at the end of the year

q: A decision package prepared for an activity under zero-base budgeting should show, in addition to the purpose and cost of the activity:

options.A: Only the expenditure incurred on the activity in the previous year
options.B: The name of the manager who first started the activity
options.C: The selling prices charged by competitors for similar work
options.D: The consequences of not performing the activity, alternative ways of performing it, and the cost and benefit of each incremental level of the activity

q: Two decision packages for the same service are drawn so that funding the higher package automatically includes the work in the lower package and adds further work to it. In ranking such packages for a limited fund, management should:

options.A: Fund the higher package first in every case, regardless of cost
options.B: Treat the two packages as wholly independent proposals competing with each other
options.C: Rank the successive increments by their cost-benefit worth, funding each increment only if its own benefit justifies its own cost
options.D: Reject both packages, since packages for one service must never overlap

q: Under zero-base budgeting, the package drawn at a level below the current level of an activity serves the specific purpose of showing management:

options.A: That the activity must be closed down altogether at the next review
options.B: What work would be lost, and what saving made, if funding were cut to that lower level, so the cut is a considered choice and not a surprise
options.C: The exact amount by which the manager's salary should be reduced
options.D: That incremental budgeting would have given a larger allotment

q: Performance budgeting in a government department classifies expenditure primarily by:

options.A: Programmes, activities and projects, linking each outlay to the physical work or service it is meant to produce
options.B: The objects of expenditure alone, such as salaries, travel and contingencies, with no reference to output
options.C: The names of the officers who are authorised to incur the expenditure
options.D: The source from which the funds for each item were received

q: A purely line-item (object-wise) budget in government fails to answer the question that performance budgeting is designed to answer, namely:

options.A: Whether the total expenditure stayed within the total grant voted
options.B: Whether proper vouchers support each item of expenditure
options.C: Whether the prescribed financial rules were followed in incurring the expenditure
options.D: What physical results were achieved, and at what unit cost, for the money spent on each programme

q: A performance budget provides Rs 48,00,000 for a programme under which 12,000 units of work are targeted. The budgeted unit cost of the work is:

options.A: Rs 40 per unit
options.B: Rs 4,000 per unit
options.C: Rs 400 per unit
options.D: Rs 250 per unit

q: For performance budgeting in government to work in practice, its essential supporting requirement is that:

options.A: Every department should be allowed to spend its grant without reporting physical progress
options.B: Suitable work norms, unit costs and a reporting system measuring physical achievement alongside financial progress are developed for each activity
options.C: The budget should be prepared only after the year's expenditure has been completed
options.D: Physical targets should be stated without any corresponding financial estimates

q: Under a rolling (continuous) budget system, when one month or quarter expires, the organisation:

options.A: Adds a fresh month or quarter at the far end, revising the intervening periods for changed conditions, so the budget always covers a full period ahead
options.B: Stops budgeting until a completely new annual budget is prepared
options.C: Merely extends the expired month's figures unchanged to the end of the year
options.D: Discards all functional budgets and retains only the cash budget

q: A rolling budget is particularly valuable where trading conditions change rapidly because:

options.A: It allows the original annual figures to remain untouched for the whole year
options.B: It removes the need to forecast anything beyond the current month
options.C: Plans are kept continuously up to date and managers always have a budget covering the coming period framed on recent conditions
options.D: It reduces the frequency with which any budget figures are reviewed

q: Budget reports sent to higher management are governed by the principle of management by exception, which means that they:

options.A: List every transaction of every department in full detail
options.B: Report favourable variances only, adverse variances being omitted
options.C: Are prepared only at the end of the financial year
options.D: Highlight the significant variances that need attention and action, rather than burdening management with all the detail

q: The flexed budget cost for the output achieved is Rs 1,85,000 and the actual cost incurred is Rs 1,94,250. The budget variance reported for control is:

options.A: Rs 9,250 favourable
options.B: Rs 9,250 adverse
options.C: Rs 3,79,250 adverse
options.D: Nil, since actual cost differs from the flexed budget

q: A well-designed periodic budget report for a budget centre shows, in sequence:

options.A: The budget (flexed for the activity achieved), the actual result, and the variance between the two, with the causes of major variances
options.B: Only the actual expenditure, the budget figures being kept confidential from the manager
options.C: The previous year's actuals and nothing else
options.D: The names of the employees whose work caused each variance

q: Revision of a budget during the period, as distinct from merely flexing it, is justified when:

options.A: Actual output in a month differs from the budgeted output, costs behaving as expected
options.B: A variance of any size, however small, appears in a monthly report
options.C: A permanent change in conditions, such as a major change in wage rates, prices or demand, has made the original budget unrealistic as a basis of control
options.D: The manager of a budget centre asks for an easier target after a poor month

q: Budgeted hours are 6,000, hours actually worked are 6,000, and the standard hours for the output produced are 4,800. The activity ratio is:

options.A: 100 per cent
options.B: 125 per cent
options.C: 120 per cent
options.D: 80 per cent

q: In reporting variances to a budget centre manager, sound practice requires that:

options.A: All variances, controllable and uncontrollable alike, be charged against the manager's performance
options.B: Variances arising from factors outside the manager's control be separately identified, so that he is judged on the variances he could influence
options.C: Uncontrollable variances be concealed from senior management as well
options.D: Variances be reported in money terms only, without any enquiry into their causes

q: A recognised limitation of budgetary control, even in a well-run system, is that:

options.A: A budget rests on estimates and forecasts which may prove inaccurate, so it must be applied with judgement and not treated as an infallible standard
options.B: Budgets can be prepared only by the accounts department working alone
options.C: Budgetary control prevents managers from exercising any initiative at all times
options.D: Budgets lose all value the moment a single variance appears

q: Once the functional budgets have been examined and co-ordinated, they are combined into the master budget, which ordinarily consists of:

options.A: The sales budget and the production budget only
options.B: A statement of the fixed assets owned by the enterprise
options.C: The budgeted profit and loss account and the budgeted balance sheet, summarising all the functional budgets
options.D: The cash budget alone, the other budgets being discarded

q: A service department's costs are mostly fixed within the year, but its workload fluctuates sharply from month to month. For controlling this department, the most appropriate arrangement is:

options.A: A fixed annual budget compared directly with each month's actual cost, without adjustment
options.B: No budget at all, since its costs are largely fixed
options.C: A budget compared only with the results of other service departments
options.D: A flexible budget that separates its fixed costs from the costs varying with workload, so each month's actual cost is judged against the allowance for that month's workload

q: A proposed additional loop line at a junction station is estimated to cost Rs 4.5 crore. It is expected to bring gross earnings of Rs 92 lakh a year, against additional working expenses of Rs 38 lakh a year. Its anticipated rate of return on the estimated cost is:

options.A: 20.4 per cent
options.B: 12 per cent
options.C: 8.4 per cent
options.D: 10 per cent

q: A crossing station proposal requires an initial outlay of Rs 24,00,000. The present value of its expected net cash inflows, discounted at the cost of capital, is Rs 27,60,000. Its Net Present Value is:

In the financial justification of a doubling proposal, the earnings of all trains that will run over the doubled section, including the trains already running on the existing single line, are claimed in full as the earnings of the work. The defect in this justification is that:

options.A: Earnings of a work must always be stated net of depreciation
options.B: Only the gross earnings, and not the net earnings, of the work may be claimed
options.C: Only the additional earnings attributable to the work itself should be counted, since the earnings of the trains already running would arise even without the work
options.D: Earnings may be claimed only for the first ten years of the work

q: A proposed new line in a backward region shows a Financial Internal Rate of Return of 6 per cent, below the prescribed test, but an Economic Internal Rate of Return of 14 per cent, the economic appraisal counting savings in travel time, fewer road accidents and regional development benefits. The correct appraisal conclusion is that the line:

options.A: Must be rejected outright, since no work failing the financial test can ever be taken up
options.B: Is financially remunerative, since its economic return exceeds the prescribed test
options.C: Has been wrongly appraised, since the economic return can never exceed the financial return
options.D: Is not financially remunerative but is economically justified, and may be taken up on socio-economic grounds with that position recorded

q: For a project, the present value of the expected benefits is Rs 57,00,000 and the present value of the expected costs is Rs 45,60,000. Its benefit-cost ratio is:

A product gives a throughput of Rs 840 per unit and occupies the bottleneck machine for 0.7 hour per unit. The total factory cost works out to Rs 800 per bottleneck hour. The Throughput Accounting Ratio of the product is:

A factory holds 12,000 units of work-in-progress on which the direct material cost is Rs 38 per unit and conversion costs of Rs 5,70,000 have also been incurred. Under throughput accounting, the work-in-progress will be valued at:
The Throughput Accounting Ratio of a product works out to less than 1. This indicates that:

options.A: The product's selling price is below its material cost
options.B: The product uses no bottleneck time at all
options.C: The product's throughput exactly equals the factory's operating expenses
options.D: The return per bottleneck hour earned by the product is less than the factory cost per bottleneck hour, so that on throughput criteria the product does not cover the operating cost of the bottleneck time it uses

q: To launch a new service in a market where competition is keen and buyers are price-sensitive, a firm deliberately fixes a low initial price, accepting a thin margin in order to capture a large share of the market quickly. This pricing strategy is known as:

options.A: Price skimming
options.B: Penetration pricing
options.C: Cost-plus pricing
options.D: Prestige pricing

q: A firm brings out a novel product that has, for the time being, no close substitute. It fixes a high initial price to earn the maximum from buyers willing to pay it, and lowers the price in stages as rival products appear. This strategy is known as:

options.A: Price skimming
options.B: Penetration pricing
options.C: Going-rate pricing
options.D: Marginal-cost pricing

q: The products of an industry are largely homogeneous and competition among sellers is keen, so that a price fixed well above the level charged by rivals would lose the firm its market. In such a situation, a firm that fixes its price mainly by reference to the prices charged by its competitors is following:

options.A: Target-return pricing
options.B: Cost-plus pricing
options.C: Going-rate pricing
options.D: Administered pricing

q: In appraising a project by the risk-adjusted discount rate method, the discount rate applied to the project is built up as:

options.A: The risk-free rate alone, risk being adjusted in the cash flows instead
options.B: The firm's average cost of debt alone
options.C: A rate that falls as the risk of the project rises
options.D: The risk-free rate plus a risk premium, the premium being larger the greater the risk perceived in the project

q: A project costing Rs 12,50,000 is expected to yield cash inflows of Rs 7,20,000 at the end of Year 1 and Rs 10,08,000 at the end of Year 2. Its risk-adjusted discount rate is 20 per cent. Its net present value at that rate is:

A firm sorts its capital projects into classes, such as replacement of existing assets, expansion of existing lines and ventures into new products, and prescribes a separate hurdle rate for each class, the rate rising from the first class to the last. The principle underlying this practice is that:

options.A: All projects of a firm should earn at least the risk-free rate
options.B: Longer-lived projects should always carry lower hurdle rates
options.C: The discount rate used in appraisal should be matched to the degree of risk of the class of project, since a single average rate would overstate the worth of risky projects and understate that of safe ones
options.D: Replacement projects should be appraised without discounting at all

q: Activity Based Management (ABM) is distinguished from Activity Based Costing (ABC) in that ABM:

options.A: Assigns overhead costs to products on the basis of a single volume-based rate
options.B: Uses the activity and cost-driver information provided by ABC to manage activities themselves, improving processes and eliminating activities that add no value
options.C: Is concerned only with the valuation of closing inventory for financial reporting
options.D: Dispenses altogether with the identification of cost drivers
